paragraphs.heading: What the word means
paragraphs.text: Decolonization is the end of colonialism, which is when imperial nations take over and rule foreign lands, often across the sea. People disagree about exactly what the word means and how to use it. Some scholars focus on independence movements in colonies and on the fall of global empires. David Strang says it is achieved when a territory becomes a sovereign state formally recognised by other nations, or is fully merged into an existing state. The United Nations puts the right to self-determination at its heart and says this right can be used with or without full independence.

paragraphs.heading: Waves of independence
paragraphs.text: As a push for colonies to break free from the countries that ruled them, decolonization began in 1775 with the American Revolution against the British Empire. During the Napoleonic Wars, revolution in Haiti, independence wars in Spanish America and Brazil's split from Portugal brought decolonization to the French, Spanish and Portuguese empires. Big waves followed after the First World War and after the Second, when many countries won independence in the years that came after. A last wave came after the Cold War, as the Soviet Union collapsed, Palau became independent, and Hong Kong and Macau were handed over. In the two centuries after 1783, 165 colonies won independence from Western powers, yet seventeen territories are still classed by the UN as non-self-governing.

paragraphs.heading: The first breakaways
paragraphs.text: The first colonies to break away were Britain's thirteen in North America, which declared independence in 1776 as the United States and beat Britain in the Revolutionary War. In the French colony of Saint-Domingue on Hispaniola, a revolt in 1789 and a slave uprising in 1791 led to Haiti's independence in 1804. When Napoleon invaded Spain, the turmoil cut Spain's direct links with its American colonies. Spain's grip on their trade was the main reason many chose independence, and the wars began with a revolt in La Paz, Bolivia, in 1809. For about fifteen years royalists and rebels fought across South America and Mexico, and many countries declared independence.

paragraphs.heading: Why it spread
paragraphs.text: Scholars give several reasons why anti-colonial movements spread. One view says that more education in the colonies led people to demand rule by the people. Marxist accounts point to economic shifts toward wage labour and a growing middle class, while others see each revolution inspiring the next. Some stress that colonies became less profitable and empires more costly. Others note that by the 20th century colonial powers faced indifferent publics at home, hostile superpowers and fewer local allies, so holding on to colonies came to feel like a burden.

paragraphs.heading: Ideas and rights
paragraphs.text: Many historians trace the ideas behind independence movements to the Age of Enlightenment. Enlightenment theories such as individualism and liberalism shaped debates over the constitutions of newly independent countries. Today's decolonial scholars criticise those same ideas for erasing Indigenous ways of knowing and for failing to give liberty, equality and dignity to marginalised and Indigenous people. In 1960 a UN General Assembly resolution described colonial rule by foreigners as a breach of human rights.

paragraphs.heading: Minds, cultures and today
paragraphs.text: The word can also mean freeing the mind from colonisers' ideas that made colonised people feel inferior. Early studies came in the 1960s and 1970s, and Frantz Fanon, a writer from Martinique, set out in The Wretched of the Earth (1961) many themes later writers took up. Later work looked at the economic inequality colonialism left behind and at the destruction of cultures, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o's Decolonising the Mind (1986) examined its effects on culture and language. These questions are still raised today: Indigenous peoples under settler colonialism keep calling for decolonization and self-determination, and in the Americas and South Africa the debate often goes by the name decoloniality.
